## 1. Here is a function that sums up our data in one go

```{R}
# Summary stats function: one call, all the numbers you care about
my_summary <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]                      # drop missing values first
  
  result <- data.frame(
    n        = length(x),
    mean     = mean(x),
    median   = median(x),
    sd       = sd(x),
    variance = var(x),
    min      = min(x),
    max      = max(x),
    range    = max(x) - min(x),
    q1       = quantile(x, 0.25, names = FALSE),
    q3       = quantile(x, 0.75, names = FALSE),
    iqr      = IQR(x)
  )
  return(round(result, 3))
}
```

```{r}
# Test drive: proving the function works on real data
my_summary(mtcars$mpg)

# Sanity check against R's built-in
summary(mtcars$mpg)
```

## 2.let's make a function that runs a two-sample t-test by hand

# Two-sample t-test function: are these two groups really different?

```{r}
my_t_test <- function(x, y) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]
  
  n1 <- length(x);  n2 <- length(y)
  m1 <- mean(x);    m2 <- mean(y)
  v1 <- var(x);     v2 <- var(y)
  
  # Welch's t-statistic (doesn't assume equal variances)
  se <- sqrt(v1/n1 + v2/n2)
  t_stat <- (m1 - m2) / se
  
  # Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
  df <- (v1/n1 + v2/n2)^2 /
        ((v1/n1)^2/(n1 - 1) + (v2/n2)^2/(n2 - 1))
  
  # Two-tailed p-value
  p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df)
  
  # 95% confidence interval for the difference in means
  ci <- (m1 - m2) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df) * se
  
  data.frame(
    mean_x = round(m1, 3),
    mean_y = round(m2, 3),
    t      = round(t_stat, 3),
    df     = round(df, 2),
    p      = signif(p_value, 4),
    ci_low = round(ci[1], 3),
    ci_high = round(ci[2], 3),
    decision = ifelse(p_value < 0.05,
                      "Reject H0: means differ",
                      "Fail to reject H0")
  )
}
```

```{r}
# Test drive: do manual and automatic cars burn different amounts of fuel?
auto   <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0]
manual <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1]

my_t_test(auto, manual)

# Sanity check against R's built-in
t.test(auto, manual)
```

## 3. functions that belong to apply family

# lapply: run a function on each column and keep the results in a list

```{R}
nums <- mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")]

lapply(nums, mean)
```

# sapply: same loop as lapply, but the answer comes back as a neat vector
```{r}
sapply(nums, mean)
```

it can also Work with our own function too, and returns a table

```{r}
sapply(nums, my_summary)
```

# tapply: average fuel use for each cylinder group

```{r}
tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, mean)
```

Another example: average mpg for automatic vs manual

```{r}
tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$am, mean)
```

# apply: summarise a matrix by rows or by columns

```{r}
m <- as.matrix(mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")])

apply(m, 2, mean)   # 2 = go down each column
apply(m, 1, sum)    # 1 = go across each row
```

# mapply: take the 1st item from each input, then the 2nd, and so on

```{r}
mapply(function(x, y) x + y, 1:5, 6:10)
```

Practical example: repeat a word a different number of times

```{r}
mapply(rep, c("a", "b", "c"), 3:1)
```

Using our own t-test idea: compare mpg with hp-scaled values pairwise

```{r}
mapply(function(a, b) round(a / b, 2), mtcars$mpg[1:5], mtcars$cyl[1:5])
```
